name: Botulinum toxin A
lead: Botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A) is a neurotoxic protein made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. It blocks release of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing temporary flaccid paralysis of the injected muscle. In heavily diluted form it is used for medical and cosmetic purposes, and commercial products include Botox Cosmetic, Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau and Daxxify [1][2].

Cosmetically it is injected to soften dynamic wrinkles, especially in the upper third of the face: glabellar (frown) lines, forehead lines and crow's feet. Wikipedia describes it as considered relatively safe and effective for this, with an effect that is usually visible three to five days after injection and lasts typically two to four months for glabellar lines, in some patients up to six months or longer [1]. Appearance-related uses discussed by clinicians also include masseter slimming and brow shaping [3][4].

Medical uses are broad, including chronic migraine, spasticity, dystonia, overactive bladder, hyperhidrosis and strabismus [1]. Every botulinum toxin label carries a boxed warning about distant spread of toxin effect, and a meta-analysis of cosmetic upper-face injections reported an overall complication rate of 16 percent, with headache, local skin reactions and facial neuromuscular symptoms the most common [2][5].

paras: Injection into the muscles beneath facial wrinkles relaxes them, smoothing the overlying skin [1]. The US label for Daxxify, for instance, is indicated for temporary improvement in the appearance of moderate to severe glabellar lines associated with corrugator or procerus activity in adults [2]. A 2025 randomized, double-blind split-face trial in 25 women tested onabotulinumtoxinA together with a hyaluronic acid skin booster (Skinvive) for moderate and severe canthal lines, evaluating efficacy and durability [6]. A registered phase 4 study tested variable doses of Dysport across the full face in sun-induced wrinkles (90 participants) [7]. International consensus recommendations address aesthetic use of a ready-to-use abobotulinumtoxinA product [8].

Facial contouring uses include injection of the masseter and combination approaches in so-called liquid facelifts, described in a 2024 review [4]. A 2020 randomized placebo-controlled trial in 30 people injected the masseter in sleep bruxism, with polysomnography before and at 4 and 12 weeks [9]. Studies in masticatory muscle pain and bruxism-related myalgia compared botulinum toxin with other approaches [10][11].

Wikipedia lists spasticity (cerebral palsy, stroke, spinal cord injury), cervical and other dystonias, strabismus, hyperhidrosis, overactive bladder and migraine; FDA approved prophylaxis of chronic migraine in 2010, while episodic migraine is not approved [1]. The PREEMPT 2 trial reported on onabotulinumtoxinA in chronic migraine [12]. Reviews cover overactive bladder, gastrointestinal uses, facial palsy synkinesis and pre-operative use for ventral hernia repair [13][14][15][16].

The toxin enters motor nerve terminals and cleaves SNAP-25, a protein needed to dock and release acetylcholine vesicles; recovery occurs gradually as nerve terminals recover from the cleavage and new endings form [2]. Earlier work showed that tetanus and botulinum-B toxins block neurotransmitter release by cleaving synaptobrevin [17]. A 2025 review covers the molecular architecture and mechanism [18]. Potency units are not interchangeable between products [2].
Literature reviews discuss immunogenicity of BoNT-A across clinical and cosmetic treatment and the factors involved in nonresponse in aesthetics [19][20].

Safety: a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of glabellar and forehead injections included 24 studies with 4,268 injection sessions and 1,234 placebos, and reported a 16 percent overall complication rate, headache, local skin reactions and facial neuromuscular symptoms being frequent. Complication odds with abobotulinumtoxin were higher than with placebo (odds ratio 1.62) [5].
Wrinkles: the periorbital split-face trial of onabotulinumtoxinA with Skinvive and the full-face Dysport dose study are the main cosmetic trials in the reference set [6][7].

Bruxism and jaw pain: a randomized placebo-controlled trial in sleep bruxism, a randomized pilot in temporomandibular masticatory pain, and a prospective comparison with dry needling, drugs and manual therapy for bruxism myalgia [9][10][11].
Melasma: a 2025 split-face randomized study examined botulinum toxin A in melasma [21].

Other registered studies cover chronic neck and back pain (60), oromandibular dystonia (240), hypertrophic scar itch (60), Raynaud's phenomenon (24), vaginismus (40) and vulvodynia (5) [22][23][24][25][26][27]. A topical botulinum eyedrop study on palpebral fissure was terminated after 2 participants [28].

The US label has a boxed warning that effects of all botulinum toxin products may spread from the injection area, with symptoms reported hours to weeks after injection; swallowing and breathing difficulties can be life-threatening and deaths have been reported, and risk is probably greatest in children treated for spasticity (an unapproved use for Daxxify) [2]. The label also lists hypersensitivity, cardiovascular adverse reactions, increased compromise in pre-existing neuromuscular disorders, dysphagia and ophthalmic adverse reactions [2]. There are no data on use in pregnant women, and animal studies showed fetal growth effects at maternally toxic doses [2].

In the cosmetic upper-face meta-analysis, the authors note that increasing popularity is met with limited regulation, potentially posing risk to patient safety [5]. Reports in the literature also describe botulinum toxin as a potential biological weapon, with consensus public-health recommendations published in JAMA in 2001 [29].

Cosmetic botulinum toxin is one of the most widely recognised aesthetic treatments. On T Nation, mentions are mostly casual: members joke about celebrities whose faces look expressionless or 'frozen' after Botox, and about injections alongside other cosmetic procedures [30][31][32]. One member reports considering Botox for a facial concern [33]. No protocol discussion appears in the forum material reviewed, so descriptions of practice here rest on clinical sources.

timeline.event: Research shows clostridial neurotoxins block neurotransmitter release by cleaving SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin) [17].
JAMA publishes consensus recommendations on botulinum toxin as a biological weapon [29].
FDA approves botulinum toxin for chronic migraine prophylaxis; PREEMPT 2 trial published [1][12].
UK MHRA approves treatment of restricted ankle motion due to lower-limb spasticity after stroke [1].
Meta-analysis reports a 16% complication rate for cosmetic glabellar and forehead injections [5].

lore.intro: In the forum material reviewed, botulinum toxin appears mostly in casual comments about celebrities and cosmetic procedures rather than in how-to threads [30][31][32].

claims.claim: Botox leaves faces frozen and unable to express emotion
claims.believers: T Nation posters remark that celebrities who use it can no longer move parts of their face, such as the upper lip, or have lost expressiveness [30][34].
claims.experts: Facial neuromuscular symptoms are among frequently reported treatment-related complications in a 2022 meta-analysis, which reported an overall complication rate of 16 percent [5]. Effects are temporary and typically last two to four months for glabellar lines [1].

claims.claim: Botox smooths dynamic wrinkles in the upper face
claims.believers: Commenters assume it is the standard injectable for lines and discuss it alongside other cosmetic procedures [31][33].
claims.experts: Product labels are indicated for temporary improvement of glabellar lines, and Wikipedia describes it as relatively safe and effective for wrinkles in the upper third of the face [1][2].

claims.claim: Botulinum toxin can slim the jaw or treat clenching
claims.believers: Jaw contouring is discussed in aesthetic circles as a use of masseter injections.
claims.experts: Randomized trials have studied masseter injection in sleep bruxism and masticatory pain, rather than cosmetic slimming outcomes [9][10][11].
